reason: E2 shows that sessile dislocations (Lomer-Cottrell locks) in the FCC phase of a dual-phase HEA hinder dislocation motion, supporting the general premise that interfaces can act as barriers. However, neither E1 nor E2 provides evidence that improving interfacial bonding quality (as opposed to inherent phase-boundary structure) enhances creep resistance, nor that thermal spray parameters can achieve this without altering other microstructural features. E1 discusses rafting and interfacial dislocation networks in conventional superalloys, not FCC/BCC HEA coatings.
premises: Phase boundaries in dual-phase HEAs can act as barriers to dislocation motion
Improved interfacial bonding enhances the barrier effect of phase boundaries
Dislocation pile-ups at interfaces delay shear localization and reduce creep rate
Thermal spray parameters can be tailored to improve interfacial bonding without altering phase fraction or grain size
Lomer-Cottrell locks in FCC matrix immobilize dislocations and enhance work hardening
